claim: ATG14 protein is expressed in all uterine compartments (luminal epithelium, glands, and stroma) by day 1 of pregnancy in mice.
source: We found distinct expression of ATG14 in all the uterine compartments (luminal epithelium, glands, and stroma) by day 1 of pregnancy, which disappeared by day 2 of pregnancy (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1A and direct statement in text.

claim: ATG14 expression in the uterus disappears by day 2 of pregnancy in mice.
source: We found distinct expression of ATG14 in all the uterine compartments (luminal epithelium, glands, and stroma) by day 1 of pregnancy, which disappeared by day 2 of pregnancy (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1A and direct statement in text.

claim: ATG14 expression in the uterus reappears by day 3 and persists through day 7 of pregnancy in mice.
source: However, the ATG14 expression in the uterus reappeared by day 3 and persisted through day 7 of pregnancy.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1A showing ATG14 expression from days 3-7.

claim: The period from day 3 to day 7 of pregnancy is critical for uterine preparation for embryo implantation and decidualization.
source: The period from day 3 to day 7 is critical as it is during this time when the uterus begins to prepare for embryo implantation and undergoes the decidualization process.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of reproductive biology and temporal correlation with ATG14 expression.

claim: Atg14 mRNA expression levels in uteri from early pregnant mice are consistent with protein expression patterns.
source: Consistent with protein expression, similar Atg14 expression at mRNA levels was noted in uteri from early pregnant mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Conditional knockout mice (Prcre/+; Atg14flox/flox) were generated by crossing Atg14flox/flox mice with mice expressing Cre recombinase under the control of progesterone receptor promoter.
source: Thus, to study the role of ATG14 in uterine function, we generated a conditional knockout (Prcre/+; Atg14flox/flox) mouse model by crossing Atg14flox/flox mice with mice expressing Cre recombinase under the control of progesterone receptor promoter (Prcre/+).
evidence: Direct description of experimental methodology.

claim: Atg14 cKO mice uteri show no gross morphological differences compared to control mice.
source: Histological examination of the uterus from adult females showed no gross morphological differences between Atg14 cKO and control mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Atg14 cKO mice have normal ovarian follicles and corpus luteum.
source: Further, we did not find any overt defects in the ovary as cKO mice had normal follicles and corpus luteum like their corresponding controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Atg14 transcript levels are efficiently depleted in uteri from cKO mice.
source: Analysis of transcript levels from the uterus, ovary, and liver showed that while Atg14 levels were efficiently depleted in uteri from cKO mice the levels were unaltered in the ovary and liver samples in control and cKO mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Atg14 transcript levels are unaltered in the ovary and liver of cKO mice compared to controls.
source: Analysis of transcript levels from the uterus, ovary, and liver showed that while Atg14 levels were efficiently depleted in uteri from cKO mice the levels were unaltered in the ovary and liver samples in control and cKO mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ATG14 is efficiently deleted in all uterine compartments (epithelium and stroma) of cKO mice.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis further confirmed the efficient deletion of ATG14 in all uterine compartments (epithelium and stroma) of cKO mice uteri compared to corresponding control groups (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Atg14 cKO females did not deliver any litter during a 6-month breeding trial.
source: We found that Atg14 cKO females did not deliver any litter during the 6-month trial period.
evidence: Supported by breeding trial data presented in Table 1 and Figure 1E.

claim: Control female (Atg14flox/flox) mice delivered an average of ~7–8 pups per litter every month.
source: However, the control female (Atg14flox/flox) mice delivered an average of ~7–8 pups per litter every month (Table 1; Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by breeding trial data presented in Table 1 and Figure 1E.

claim: Atg14 plays an indispensable role in female fertility with intact ovarian function.
source: These findings suggest an indispensable role of Atg14 in female fertility with intact ovarian function.
evidence: Inferred from complete infertility of cKO mice despite normal ovarian morphology.

claim: No implantation sites were observed in the uteri of Atg14 cKO females at day 5 post coitum.
source: Analysis of the implanting embryos at day 5 of pregnancy showed no implantation sites in the uteri of Atg14 cKO females, whereas ~8–9 implantation sites were seen in the uteri of control mice at 5 days post coitum (dpc) (Figure 2A, left panel).
evidence: Supported by gross morphology and histological data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Control mice uteri showed ~8–9 implantation sites at 5 days post coitum.
source: Analysis of the implanting embryos at day 5 of pregnancy showed no implantation sites in the uteri of Atg14 cKO females, whereas ~8–9 implantation sites were seen in the uteri of control mice at 5 days post coitum (dpc) (Figure 2A, left panel).
evidence: Supported by gross morphology data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No embryos were present in the uterine lumen of Atg14 cKO mice at 5 dpc.
source: While there was no embryo present in the uterine lumen of Atg14 cKO mice, a fully attached embryo encapsulated by the luminal uterine epithelium was seen in control mice uteri (Figure 2A, middle panel).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A fully attached embryo encapsulated by the luminal uterine epithelium was seen in control mice uteri at 5 dpc.
source: While there was no embryo present in the uterine lumen of Atg14 cKO mice, a fully attached embryo encapsulated by the luminal uterine epithelium was seen in control mice uteri (Figure 2A, middle panel).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: MUC1 expression persisted in the luminal epithelium of cKO mice uteri at 5 dpc and 4 dpc.
source: Additionally, MUC1, a receptive marker expression, persisted in the luminal epithelium of cKO mice uteri at 5 dpc as well as 4 dpc (Figure 2A, right panel, Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2C.

claim: Successful embryo attachment and implantation requires a transition from a non-receptive to a receptive state orchestrated by steroid hormones.
source: The process of successful embryo attachment and implantation within the uterus necessitates a transition from a non-receptive to a receptive state, a transformation orchestrated under the regulated influence of steroid hormones.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of reproductive biology.

claim: Uteri from both Atg14 control and cKO mice showed similar proliferation in response to E2 treatment as evidenced by Ki-67 staining.
source: In response to E2 treatment, uteri from both Atg14 control and cKO mice showed similar proliferation as evidenced by Ki-67 staining (Figure 2B, middle panel).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Following E2 + P4 co-stimulation, epithelial proliferation was inhibited with concomitant induction of stromal cell proliferation in control mice uteri.
source: Following the co-stimulation with E2 + P4 treatment, epithelial proliferation was inhibited with concomitant induction of stromal cell proliferation in control mice uteri indicating fully receptive uteri (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Atg14 cKO mice uteri failed to elicit sub-epithelial stromal cell proliferation following E2 + P4 treatment.
source: Interestingly, cKO mice uteri failed to elicit sub-epithelial stromal cell proliferation and showed intact P4-driven inhibition of epithelial proliferation.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Atg14 cKO mice uteri showed intact P4-driven inhibition of epithelial proliferation.
source: Interestingly, cKO mice uteri failed to elicit sub-epithelial stromal cell proliferation and showed intact P4-driven inhibition of epithelial proliferation.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Uteri from Atg14 cKO mice at 4 dpc showed a reduced number of proliferating stromal cells.
source: Consistently, uteri from Atg14 cKO mice at 4 dpc showed a reduced number of proliferating stromal cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There were no significant changes in E2-induced targets (Lif, Mcm2, Ccnd1, and Fgf18) at 4 dpc in Atg14 cKO mice.
source: The absence of significant changes in E2-induced targets, such as Lif, Mcm2, Ccnd1, and Fgf18, at 4 dpc (Figure 2E) supports our conclusion that ATG14 is required for P4-mediated but not for E2-mediated actions during uterine receptivity.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: ATG14 is required for P4-mediated but not for E2-mediated actions during uterine receptivity.
source: The absence of significant changes in E2-induced targets, such as Lif, Mcm2, Ccnd1, and Fgf18, at 4 dpc (Figure 2E) supports our conclusion that ATG14 is required for P4-mediated but not for E2-mediated actions during uterine receptivity.
evidence: Inferred from differential responses to E2 vs E2+P4 treatments and gene expression data.

claim: Serum levels of E2 and P4 at D4 of pregnancy are normal in Atg14 cKO mice.
source: Moreover, the normal serum levels of E2 and P4 at D4 of pregnancy rule out any hormonal imbalances, strongly suggesting that the observed phenotype is primarily due to the uterine-specific loss of Atg14 (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The observed phenotype in Atg14 cKO mice is primarily due to uterine-specific loss of Atg14 rather than hormonal imbalances.
source: Moreover, the normal serum levels of E2 and P4 at D4 of pregnancy rule out any hormonal imbalances, strongly suggesting that the observed phenotype is primarily due to the uterine-specific loss of Atg14 (Figure 2F).
evidence: Inferred from normal hormone levels combined with tissue-specific knockout design.

claim: Only 1–2% of embryos were retrieved from Atg14 cKO mice uteri on day 4 of pregnancy.
source: Interestingly, in cKO mice, we could retrieve only 1–2% of embryos from their uteri, whereas in control mice, 100% of well-developed blastocysts were retrieved from their uteri (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by embryo flushing data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: 100% of well-developed blastocysts were retrieved from control mice uteri on day 4 of pregnancy.
source: Interestingly, in cKO mice, we could retrieve only 1–2% of embryos from their uteri, whereas in control mice, 100% of well-developed blastocysts were retrieved from their uteri (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by embryo flushing data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: No embryos or blastocysts were recovered from control mice oviduct flushing on day 4 of pregnancy.
source: As expected, in the control mice oviduct flushing, we could not recover any embryos or blastocysts, indicating their precise and timely transport to the uterus.
evidence: Supported by embryo flushing data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Approximately 90% of embryos were retrieved from Atg14 cKO mice oviducts on day 4 of pregnancy.
source: Unexpectedly, oviduct flushing from cKO mice resulted in the retrieval of approximately 90% of embryos, suggesting their potential entrapment within the oviducts, impeding their transit to the uterus (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by embryo flushing data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Embryos are entrapped within the oviducts of Atg14 cKO mice, impeding their transit to the uterus.
source: Unexpectedly, oviduct flushing from cKO mice resulted in the retrieval of approximately 90% of embryos, suggesting their potential entrapment within the oviducts, impeding their transit to the uterus (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Inferred from the high percentage of embryos recovered from oviducts rather than uteri.

claim: There was no significant difference in the average number of blastocysts, morula, or nonviable embryos retrieved from Atg14 control uteri and cKO oviducts at 4 dpc.
source: At 4 dpc, there was no significant difference in the average number of blastocysts, morula, or nonviable or retrieved from Atg14 control uteri and cKO oviducts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by embryo counting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The percentage of developmentally delayed embryos appeared to be higher in Atg14 cKO oviducts compared to embryos retrieved from control uteri.
source: However, we noted that the percentage of developmentally delayed embryos appeared to be higher in Atg14 cKO oviducts compared to the embryos retrieved from control uteri (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by embryo staging data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: An entrapped embryo was observed in the ampulla of Atg14 cKO oviduct at 4 dpc.
source: The histological analysis further confirmed an entrapped embryo in the ampulla of Atg14 cKO at 4 dpc as shown in Figure 3D.
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: PR-cre activity is present in the isthmus of the oviduct.
source: Given the embryo retention phenotype in oviduct, we sought to determine if ATG14 is expressed in this region. Consistent with previous studies reporting PR-cre activity in the isthmus (Herrera et al., 2020; Soyal et al., 2005), we found a significant depletion of ATG14 in the isthmus compared to the ampulla (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous studies and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: ATG14 is significantly depleted in the isthmus compared to the ampulla in Atg14 cKO mice.
source: Consistent with previous studies reporting PR-cre activity in the isthmus (Herrera et al., 2020; Soyal et al., 2005), we found a significant depletion of ATG14 in the isthmus compared to the ampulla (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Increased p62 and LC3B expression in cKO oviducts suggests that the embryo retention phenotype might be attributed to the loss of ATG14-dependent autophagy.
source: Further, the increased p62 and LC3B expression in cKO oviducts suggests that the observed embryo retention phenotype might be attributed to the loss of ATG14-dependent autophagy in cKO oviducts (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and inference from autophagy markers.

claim: Atg14 cKO mice oviduct lining shows marked eosinophilic cytoplasmic change akin to decidualization in human oviducts.
source: The cKO mice oviduct lining shows marked eosinophilic cytoplasmic change akin to decidualization in human oviducts.
evidence: Based on histological observations described in the text.

claim: Some cells in Atg14 cKO oviducts showed degenerative changes with cytoplasmic vacuolization and nuclear pyknosis, loss of nuclear polarity, and loss of distinct cell borders.
source: Some of the cells showed degenerative changes with cytoplasmic vacuolization and nuclear pyknosis, loss of nuclear polarity, and loss of distinct cell borders giving an appearance of fusion of cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by histological observations shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Marked cytologic enlargement in Atg14 cKO oviducts causes luminal obliteration or narrowing resulting in a completely unorganized, obstructed, and narrow lumen.
source: The marked cytologic enlargement appears to cause luminal obliteration or narrowing resulting in a completely unorganized, obstructed, and narrow lumen, thereby hampering the path of embryos to reach the uterus as evident from an entrapped embryo shown in Figure 3D.
evidence: Inferred from histological observations and correlation with embryo entrapment.

claim: Atg14 cKO oviducts have completely distorted epithelial structures with loss of epithelial cell integrity.
source: Further, epithelial (cytokeratin KRT8-positive) and myosalpinx (α-smooth muscle active [SMA]-positive) marker analysis revealed completely distorted epithelial structures (in terms of loss of epithelial cell integrity) with no overt defects in the muscle organization in oviducts of cKO mice (Figure 3F, lower panel).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: There are no overt defects in muscle organization in oviducts of Atg14 cKO mice.
source: Further, epithelial (cytokeratin KRT8-positive) and myosalpinx (α-smooth muscle active [SMA]-positive) marker analysis revealed completely distorted epithelial structures (in terms of loss of epithelial cell integrity) with no overt defects in the muscle organization in oviducts of cKO mice (Figure 3F, lower panel).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The ampullary region from Atg14 cKO oviducts appears normal with intact epithelial and smooth muscle structures.
source: Notably, the ampullary region from cKO oviducts seems to be normal with intact epithelial and smooth muscle structures as evident from KRT8 and SMA staining (Figure 3F, upper panel).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The oviduct epithelium primarily consists of two types of cells: ciliated and secretory (non-ciliated) cells.
source: The oviduct epithelium primarily consists of two types of cells: ciliated and secretory (non-ciliated) cells.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of oviduct anatomy.

claim: Ciliated cells play a role in embryo and oocyte transport by means of ciliary beat.
source: Ciliated cells play a role in embryo and oocyte transport by means of ciliary beat and non-ciliated/secretory cells produce an oviductal fluid that is rich in amino acids and various molecules, thereby providing an optimal microenvironment for sperm capacitation, fertilization, embryonic survival, and development (Ito et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ito et al., 2020.

claim: Non-ciliated/secretory cells produce oviductal fluid that is rich in amino acids and various molecules, providing an optimal microenvironment for sperm capacitation, fertilization, embryonic survival, and development.
source: Ciliated cells play a role in embryo and oocyte transport by means of ciliary beat and non-ciliated/secretory cells produce an oviductal fluid that is rich in amino acids and various molecules, thereby providing an optimal microenvironment for sperm capacitation, fertilization, embryonic survival, and development (Ito et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ito et al., 2020.

claim: Normal ciliary structures were observed in the ampulla of both control and cKO oviducts.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, normal ciliary structures were observed in the ampulla of both control and cKO oviducts.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A reduction in both FOXJ1- and PAX8-expressing cells was observed in the isthmus of cKO oviducts.
source: However, in the isthmus of cKO oviducts, we observed a reduction in both FOXJ1- and PAX8-expressing cells (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Foxj1cre/+; Atg14flox/flox mice were generated to ablate Atg14 only in ciliary epithelial cells.
source: To address this, we generated a Foxj1cre/+; Atg14flox/flox mouse model, wherein Atg14 will be ablated only in ciliary epithelial cells.
evidence: Direct description of experimental methodology.

claim: Ciliated epithelial cells positive for acetylated α-tubulin staining did not appear to be different in Foxj1Cre/+; Atg14flox/flox mice oviduct compared to controls.
source: We observed that ciliated epithelial cells that were positive for acetylated α-tubulin staining did not appear to be different in Foxj1Cre/+; Atg14flox/flox mice oviduct compared to controls, suggesting normal ciliogenesis in Foxj1Cre/+; Atg14flox/flox mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Normal ciliogenesis occurs in Foxj1Cre/+; Atg14flox/flox mice.
source: We observed that ciliated epithelial cells that were positive for acetylated α-tubulin staining did not appear to be different in Foxj1Cre/+; Atg14flox/flox mice oviduct compared to controls, suggesting normal ciliogenesis in Foxj1Cre/+; Atg14flox/flox mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: Inferred from normal acetylated α-tubulin staining in ciliated cells.

claim: Loss of Atg14 in oviductal cilia had no impact on fertility based on a 6-month breeding trial.
source: The 6-month breeding trial revealed that loss of Atg14 in oviductal cilia had no impact on fertility (Table 2, Figure 4D and E).
evidence: Supported by breeding trial data presented in Table 2 and Figure 4D and E.

claim: Foxj1/Atg14 cKO mice showed ~7–8 visible embryo implantation sites at D5, similar to controls.
source: Consistently, D5 implantation study analysis showed ~7–8 visible embryo implantation sites in Foxj1/Atg14 cKO mice like their corresponding controls, suggesting that embryos were able to make their way to the uterus in a timely manner and undergo implantation despite the ablation of Atg14 in the oviduct ciliary epithelial cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by implantation site visualization data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Embryos were able to reach the uterus in a timely manner and undergo implantation in Foxj1/Atg14 cKO mice despite the ablation of Atg14 in oviduct ciliary epithelial cells.
source: Consistently, D5 implantation study analysis showed ~7–8 visible embryo implantation sites in Foxj1/Atg14 cKO mice like their corresponding controls, suggesting that embryos were able to make their way to the uterus in a timely manner and undergo implantation despite the ablation of Atg14 in the oviduct ciliary epithelial cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: Inferred from normal implantation sites in Foxj1/Atg14 cKO mice.

claim: Ciliary expression of Atg14 is dispensable for embryo transport.
source: These findings suggest that ciliary expression of Atg14 is dispensable for embryo transport.
evidence: Inferred from normal fertility and embryo transport in Foxj1/Atg14 cKO mice.

claim: Oviducts from Atg14 cKO females had numerous altered mitochondrial structures with abnormally enlarged mitochondria and a less dense matrix.
source: Interestingly, oviducts from cKO females had numerous altered mitochondrial structures with abnormally enlarged mitochondria and a less dense matrix compared to control oviducts that had small and compact mitochondria with tight cristae and a dense matrix (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Control oviducts had small and compact mitochondria with tight cristae and a dense matrix.
source: Interestingly, oviducts from cKO females had numerous altered mitochondrial structures with abnormally enlarged mitochondria and a less dense matrix compared to control oviducts that had small and compact mitochondria with tight cristae and a dense matrix (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Marked reductions of mitochondria network (TOM20 staining) were observed in the sub-nuclear region of oviducts from Atg14 cKO mice.
source: Corroborating and extending those findings, we observed marked reductions of mitochondria network (as defined by TOM20 staining) in the sub-nuclear region of oviducts from Atg14 cKO mice compared to more densely packed mitochondrial network in the sub-nuclear region of control ones (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Control oviducts have a more densely packed mitochondrial network in the sub-nuclear region.
source: Corroborating and extending those findings, we observed marked reductions of mitochondria network (as defined by TOM20 staining) in the sub-nuclear region of oviducts from Atg14 cKO mice compared to more densely packed mitochondrial network in the sub-nuclear region of control ones (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Uniform co-localization of cytochrome C with the TOM20-positive mitochondrial network was observed in control oviducts, reflecting intact mitochondrial integrity.
source: Further co-localization study analysis revealed a uniform co-localization of cytochrome C with the TOM20-positive mitochondrial network in control oviducts reflecting the intact mitochondrial integrity (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence co-localization data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In Atg14 cKO oviducts, cells with disrupted mitochondrial networks exhibited increased cytosolic leakage of cytochrome C.
source: In contrast, in Atg14 cKO oviducts, cells with disrupted mitochondrial networks exhibited increased cytosolic leakage of cytochrome C (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Mitochondrial functional and architecture markers (Cox4i2, Pink1, Opa1, and Drp1) showed reduced expression in Atg14 cKO oviducts compared to controls.
source: Additionally, analysis of various mitochondrial functional and architecture markers (Cox4i2, Pink1, Opa1, and Drp1) showed reduced expression in Atg14 cKO compared to controls (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Altered mitochondrial structures have been linked to the activation of pyroptosis.
source: Since we found mitochondrial defects with ATG14 loss and altered mitochondrial structures have been linked to the activation of pyroptosis, we determined if ATG14 regulates pyroptosis in the oviduct (Liu et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2019b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Liu et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2019b.

claim: A remarkable upregulation in GSDMD and caspase-1 expression was observed in Atg14 cKO oviducts compared to controls.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis revealed a remarkable upregulation in GSDMD and caspase-1 expression in the cKO oviducts compared to controls (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: No induction in GSDMD expression was observed in uterus and ovary of Atg14 cKO mice compared to controls.
source: However, histological analysis of uterus and ovary showed no induction in GSDMD expression compared to their corresponding controls (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Western blot analysis confirmed elevated expression of caspase-1 and GSDMD in cKO oviducts compared to control oviducts.
source: Western blot analysis further confirmed elevated expression of caspase-1 and GSDMD in cKO oviducts in comparison to control oviducts as shown in Figure 5G.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Elevated levels of inflammatory markers (Tnfa and Cxcr3) were observed in cKO oviducts compared to control ones.
source: Additionally, the qPCR analysis demonstrated elevated levels of inflammatory markers, such as Tnfa and Cxcr3, in cKO oviducts compared to control ones (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Atg14 plays a crucial role in regulating the pyroptotic pathway by preserving mitochondrial structural and functional integrity in the oviduct.
source: Based on these findings, we posit that Atg14 plays a crucial role in regulating the pyroptotic pathway by preserving the mitochondrial structural and functional integrity in the oviduct.
evidence: Inferred from mitochondrial defects and pyroptosis activation in Atg14 cKO oviducts.

claim: Pregnant females treated with polyphyllin VI showed ~50% embryo retention in the oviduct.
source: We found that pregnant females treated with polyphyllin VI showed ~50% embryo retention in the oviduct, whereas in the vehicle-treated group, no embryos were retained in the oviduct (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Supported by embryo flushing data shown in Figure 6A–C.

claim: In vehicle-treated pregnant females, no embryos were retained in the oviduct.
source: We found that pregnant females treated with polyphyllin VI showed ~50% embryo retention in the oviduct, whereas in the vehicle-treated group, no embryos were retained in the oviduct (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Supported by embryo flushing data shown in Figure 6A–C.

claim: Embryos retrieved from polyphyllin-treated oviducts showed more percentage of developmentally delayed and non-viable embryos compared to embryos recovered from control uteri.
source: Further analysis of embryos retrieved from polyphyllin-treated oviducts showed more percentage of developmentally delayed and non-viable embryos compared to embryos recovered from control uteri (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by embryo staging data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The average number of embryos recovered from polyphyllin- and vehicle-treated mice was not significantly different.
source: The average number of embryos recovered from polyphyllin- and vehicle-treated mice was not significantly different (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by embryo counting data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Polyphyllin VI treatment induced marked GSDMD expression in oviducts compared to vehicle-treated mice.
source: Histological analysis showed a marked induction in GSDMD expression compared to vehicle-treated mice oviducts (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Unscheduled pyroptosis adversely affects embryo transport through the oviduct.
source: Nonetheless, our findings provide evidence that unscheduled pyroptosis adversely affects embryo transport through the oviduct.
evidence: Inferred from polyphyllin VI treatment results showing embryo retention and pyroptosis activation.

claim: Atg14 safeguards against pyroptosis activation in the oviduct and allows the smooth transport of embryos to the uterus.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that Atg14 safeguards pyroptosis activation in the oviduct and allows the smooth transport of embryos to the uterus (Figure 6F).
evidence: Inferred from genetic and pharmacological evidence showing pyroptosis activation impairs embryo transport.

claim: Recurrent pregnancy loss is characterized by two or more failed clinical pregnancies.
source: Recurrent pregnancy loss, characterized by two or more failed clinical pregnancies, poses a significant challenge to reproductive health.
evidence: Based on established clinical definition.

claim: Proper oviduct function is essential for successful pregnancy establishment.
source: In addition to embryo quality and endometrial function, proper oviduct function is also essential for successful pregnancy establishment.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of reproductive biology.

claim: Structural abnormalities or inflammation resulting from infection in the oviduct may impede the transport of embryos to the endometrium, thereby increasing the risk of miscarriage.
source: Therefore, structural abnormalities or inflammation resulting from infection in the oviduct may impede the transport of embryos to the endometrium, thereby increasing the risk of miscarriage.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the role of oviduct in embryo transport.

claim: The oviduct is divided into four evolutionarily conserved regions: the infundibulum, ampulla, isthmus, and UTJ.
source: Morphologically, the oviduct is divided into four evolutionarily conserved regions: the infundibulum (nearest the ovary), ampulla (the site of fertilization), isthmus (serving as a sperm reservoir and site for early embryonic development), and UTJ (connected to the uterus).
evidence: Based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The infundibulum is nearest the ovary.
source: Morphologically, the oviduct is divided into four evolutionarily conserved regions: the infundibulum (nearest the ovary), ampulla (the site of fertilization), isthmus (serving as a sperm reservoir and site for early embryonic development), and UTJ (connected to the uterus).
evidence: Based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The ampulla is the site of fertilization.
source: Morphologically, the oviduct is divided into four evolutionarily conserved regions: the infundibulum (nearest the ovary), ampulla (the site of fertilization), isthmus (serving as a sperm reservoir and site for early embryonic development), and UTJ (connected to the uterus).
evidence: Based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The isthmus serves as a sperm reservoir and site for early embryonic development.
source: Morphologically, the oviduct is divided into four evolutionarily conserved regions: the infundibulum (nearest the ovary), ampulla (the site of fertilization), isthmus (serving as a sperm reservoir and site for early embryonic development), and UTJ (connected to the uterus).
evidence: Based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The UTJ is connected to the uterus.
source: Morphologically, the oviduct is divided into four evolutionarily conserved regions: the infundibulum (nearest the ovary), ampulla (the site of fertilization), isthmus (serving as a sperm reservoir and site for early embryonic development), and UTJ (connected to the uterus).
evidence: Based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Each segment of the oviduct comprises epithelial, stromal, and smooth muscle cells with lumen lined up with an epithelium containing secretory (PAX8+) and multi-ciliated (FOXJ1+) cells.
source: Each of these segments comprises epithelial, stromal, and smooth muscle cells with lumen lined up with an epithelium containing secretory (PAX8+) and multi-ciliated (FOXJ1+) cells.
evidence: Based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The infundibulum and ampulla are composed of more ciliated than secretory cells.
source: While the infundibulum and ampulla are composed of more ciliated than secretory cells, the isthmus has more secretory than ciliated cells (Dirksen and Satir, 1972; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dirksen and Satir, 1972; Li et al., 2017.

claim: The isthmus has more secretory than ciliated cells.
source: While the infundibulum and ampulla are composed of more ciliated than secretory cells, the isthmus has more secretory than ciliated cells (Dirksen and Satir, 1972; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dirksen and Satir, 1972; Li et al., 2017.

claim: Successful pregnancy requires embryo transit through the entire oviduct orchestrated by secretory cells producing oviduct fluid, beating cilia ensuring unidirectional flow, and periodic contractions of surrounding muscle.
source: Successful pregnancy requires that the embryo transit the entire oviduct orchestrated by the following: (1) secretory cells producing oviduct fluid, (2) beating cilia to ensure unidirectional flow of the fluid, and (3) periodic contractions of surrounding muscle to propel fluid flow.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of oviduct physiology.

claim: A combination of ciliary and muscular activity contributes to the overall success of oviduct embryo transport.
source: Therefore, a combination of ciliary and muscular activity contributes to the overall success of oviduct embryo transport.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of oviduct physiology.

claim: Impaired oviductal transport of embryos can lead to pregnancy failure and cause infertility in mice.
source: Previous studies have reported that impaired oviductal transport of embryos can lead to pregnancy failure and cause infertility in mice (Jiang et al., 2022; Herrera et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2004; Qian et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jiang et al., 2022; Herrera et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2004; Qian et al., 2018.

claim: Autophagy is a cellular process, evolutionarily conserved from yeast to mammals, that recycles long-lived proteins and organelles to maintain cell energy homeostasis.
source: Autophagy is a cellular process, evolutionarily conserved from yeast to mammals, that recycles long-lived proteins and organelles to maintain cell energy homeostasis.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of autophagy.

claim: Genetic screens for autophagy-defective mutants have currently identified 41 autophagy-related (ATG) genes.
source: Genetic screens for autophagy-defective mutants in yeast and other fungi have currently identified 41 autophagy-related (ATG) genes that play a primary role in autophagy (Klionsky, 2007; Wen and Klionsky, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Klionsky, 2007; Wen and Klionsky, 2016.

claim: Approximately half of the 41 ATG genes have homologs in higher organisms.
source: Approximately half of these genes have homologs in higher organisms, and Atg14 (also known as Barkor for Beclin 1 [Becn1]-associated autophagy-related key regulator) is one of them (Itakura et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Itakura et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2008.

claim: Atg14 is also known as Barkor (Beclin 1-associated autophagy-related key regulator).
source: Approximately half of these genes have homologs in higher organisms, and Atg14 (also known as Barkor for Beclin 1 [Becn1]-associated autophagy-related key regulator) is one of them (Itakura et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Itakura et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2008.

claim: ATG14 is part of a protein complex composed of Beclin 1, VPS15, and VPS34.
source: ATG14 is part of a protein complex that is composed of Beclin 1, vacuolar sorting protein 15 (VPS15), and VPS34 (also named as Pik3c3, the catalytic subunit of the class III phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase), and this ATG14-containing complex plays an important role in the initiation process of autophagy.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of autophagy protein complexes.

claim: VPS34 is also named Pik3c3, the catalytic subunit of the class III phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase.
source: ATG14 is part of a protein complex that is composed of Beclin 1, vacuolar sorting protein 15 (VPS15), and VPS34 (also named as Pik3c3, the catalytic subunit of the class III phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase), and this ATG14-containing complex plays an important role in the initiation process of autophagy.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of autophagy protein complexes.

claim: The ATG14-containing complex plays an important role in the initiation process of autophagy.
source: ATG14 is part of a protein complex that is composed of Beclin 1, vacuolar sorting protein 15 (VPS15), and VPS34 (also named as Pik3c3, the catalytic subunit of the class III phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase), and this ATG14-containing complex plays an important role in the initiation process of autophagy.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of autophagy protein complexes.

claim: Pyroptosis is a type of inflammatory cell death mediated by gasdermin (GSDM).
source: Pyroptosis is a type of inflammatory cell death mediated by gasdermin (GSDM) and is a product of continuous cell expansion until the cytomembrane ruptures, resulting in the release of cellular contents that can activate strong inflammatory and immune responses.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of pyroptosis.

claim: GSDM family proteins are the primary executioners of pyroptosis.
source: GSDM family proteins are the primary executioners of pyroptosis.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of pyroptosis.

claim: Cytotoxic N-terminal of GSDMs generated from caspase-mediated cleavage oligomerizes and forms pores across the cell membrane, leading to the release of proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β and IL-18.
source: Cytotoxic N-terminal of GSDMs generated from caspase-mediated cleavage of GSDM proteins oligomerizes and forms pores across the cell membrane, leading to the release of proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1β (IL-1β) and interleukin-18 (IL-18).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of pyroptosis mechanism.

claim: Aberrant activation of pyroptosis has been implicated in the progression of many diseases, including cancer and autoimmune, cardiovascular, and infectious diseases.
source: Aberrant activation of pyroptosis has been implicated in the progression of many diseases, including cancer and autoimmune, cardiovascular, and infectious diseases (Wang et al., 2019a; Man et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2019a; Man et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2022.

claim: Interactions between pyroptosis and autophagy play an important role in various physiological and pathological processes.
source: Recent studies have shown that the interactions between pyroptosis and autophagy play an important role in various physiological and pathological processes (Wang et al., 2019a; Man et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2019a; Man et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2022.

claim: Autophagy inhibition upregulates galangin-induced pyroptosis in human glioblastoma multiforme cells.
source: For example, autophagy inhibition upregulates galangin-induced pyroptosis in human glioblastoma multiforme cells and promotes pneumococcus-induced pyroptosis (Kong et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kong et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2015.

claim: Autophagy inhibition promotes pneumococcus-induced pyroptosis.
source: For example, autophagy inhibition upregulates galangin-induced pyroptosis in human glioblastoma multiforme cells and promotes pneumococcus-induced pyroptosis (Kong et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kong et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2015.

claim: Mice deficient in key autophagy genes such as Atg7 or Becn1 result in primary ovarian insufficiency and reduced progesterone production.
source: For example, mice deficient in key autophagy genes such as genetic knockout of Atg7 or Becn1 result in primary ovarian insufficiency and reduced progesterone production (Song et al., 2015; Gawriluk et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Song et al., 2015; Gawriluk et al., 2014.

claim: Atg16l, Fip200/Rb1cc1, and Becn1 play roles in endometrial physiological processes, including receptivity and decidualization.
source: Similarly, recent studies from our group established the roles of three different autophagy-specific genes: Atg16l, Fip200/Rb1cc1, or Becn1 in endometrial physiological processes, including receptivity and decidualization (Oestreich et al., 2020a; Popli et al., 2023; Oestreich et al., 2020b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Oestreich et al., 2020a; Popli et al., 2023; Oestreich et al., 2020b.

claim: Atg16l, Fip200/Rb1cc1, and Becn1 exhibited no discernible impact on oviduct function.
source: However, none of these genes exhibited any discernible impact on oviduct function.
evidence: Inferred from previous studies by the authors showing no oviduct phenotypes.

claim: ATG14 has a critical role in maintaining proper oviduct function, specifically enabling the transport of embryos to the uterus.
source: Surprisingly, in this study, we revealed a critical role for ATG14 in maintaining proper oviduct function, specifically enabling the transport of embryos to the uterus—a function distinct from that of other autophagy-related proteins.
evidence: Inferred from the unique oviduct phenotype observed with ATG14 loss.

claim: Loss of ATG14 in the oviduct resulted in severe structural abnormalities, compromising its cellular integrity, and ultimately leading to embryo retention and infertility.
source: Loss of ATG14 in the oviduct resulted in severe structural abnormalities, compromising its cellular integrity, and ultimately leading to embryo retention and infertility.
evidence: Supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including histology, embryo flushing, and breeding trials.

claim: Atg14flox/flox mice were provided by Dr. Shizuo Akira at the Department of Host Defense, Research Institute for Microbial Diseases (RIMD), Osaka University.
source: Atg14flox/flox mice were provided by a gift from Dr. Shizuo Akira at the Department of Host Defense, Research Institute for Microbial Diseases (RIMD), Osaka University, and previously described (Matsunaga et al., 2009).
evidence: Direct statement of mouse line source and citation to Matsunaga et al., 2009.

claim: Wild-type Pr-cre mice were provided by Dr. John Lydon at Baylor College of Medicine, Houston.
source: Wild-type Pr-cre mice were provided by Dr. John Lydon at Baylor College of Medicine, Houston, and previously described (Soyal et al., 2005).
evidence: Direct statement of mouse line source and citation to Soyal et al., 2005.

claim: Foxj1-cre mice were a generous gift from Dr. Michael J. Holtzman at Washington University St. Louis.
source: Foxj1-cre mice were a generous gift from Dr. Michael J. Holtzman at Washington University St. Louis and previously described (Zhang et al., 2007).
evidence: Direct statement of mouse line source and citation to Zhang et al., 2007.

claim: Polyphyllin VI is a pharmacological agent that induces caspase-1-mediated pyroptosis.
source: Polyphyllin VI (Selleck Chemicals, Houston, TX), a pharmacological agent that induces caspase-1-mediated pyroptosis, was used to study its effects on embryo transport in the oviduct (Teng et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Teng et al., 2020.

claim: Autophagy prevents mitochondrial reactive oxygen species release that can activate the inflammasome by inhibiting IL1-β and IL-18 production through the digestion of dysfunctional mitochondria.
source: For example, first, autophagy prevents mitochondrial reactive oxygen species release that can activate the inflammasome by inhibiting IL1-β and IL-18 production through the digestion of dysfunctional mitochondria (Netea-Maier et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Netea-Maier et al., 2016.

claim: Autophagy is capable of targeting inflammasome complexes for degradation, which prevents the cleavage of pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into biologically active forms.
source: Second, autophagy is capable of targeting inflammasome complexes for degradation, which prevents the cleavage of pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into biologically active forms.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of autophagy-inflammasome interactions.

claim: Autophagy machinery regulates IL-1β levels by engulfing and degrading pro-IL-1β proteins.
source: Finally, autophagy machinery further regulates IL-1β levels by engulfing and degrading pro-IL-1β proteins (Netea-Maier et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Netea-Maier et al., 2016.

claim: Sperm induce pro-inflammatory conditions in the oviduct, which are preceded by an anti-inflammatory response triggered by the presence of embryos.
source: A recent study by Finnerty et al., 2024 reported that sperm induce pro-inflammatory conditions in the oviduct, which are preceded by an anti-inflammatory response triggered by the presence of embryos (Finnerty et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Finnerty et al., 2024.

claim: Mice lacking the autophagy genes Atg14, Fip200, Atg5, or Atg7 in myeloid cells had more pronounced lung inflammation.
source: In vivo studies also found that mice lacking the autophagy genes Atg14, Fip200, Atg5, or Atg7 in myeloid cells had more pronounced lung inflammation (Lu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lu et al., 2016.

claim: Cellular swelling and fused membranous structures are unique features of activation of pyroptosis.
source: In our study, cellular swelling and fused membranous structures (a unique feature of activation of pyroptosis) were observed in the oviductal epithelial folds from Atg14 cKO mice.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of pyroptosis morphology.

claim: The induction of pyroptosis in the absence of ATG14 is specifically localized to the oviducts, with no parallel activation detected in either the ovary or uterus.
source: Notably, the induction of pyroptosis in the absence of ATG14 is specifically localized to the oviducts, with no parallel activation detected in either the ovary or uterus.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data showing tissue-specific GSDMD expression.

claim: Conditional ablation of Fip200 and Atg16l in the uterus displayed fertility defects owing to impaired implantation, uterine receptivity, and decidualization defects.
source: Conditional ablation of Fip200 and Atg16l in the uterus displayed fertility defects owing to impaired implantation, uterine receptivity, and decidualization defects.
evidence: Based on previous studies by the authors.

claim: Loss of Beclin1 in the uterus caused progressive loss of endometrial progenitor stem cells, resulting in severe uterine developmental defects and rendering the mice infertile.
source: On the contrary, loss of Beclin1 in the uterus caused progressive loss of endometrial progenitor stem cells, resulting in severe uterine developmental defects and rendering the mice infertile (Popli et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Popli et al., 2023.

claim: The absence of ATG14 did not affect the tissue integrity of the uterus.
source: It is intriguing to note that the absence of ATG14 did not affect the tissue integrity of the uterus.
evidence: Supported by histological data showing normal uterine morphology in cKO mice.

claim: ATG14's distinctive role, unlike other autophagy proteins, might be due to its pivotal role in the assembly of PtdIns3K complexes.
source: This distinctive role of ATG14, unlike other autophagy proteins, might be due to its pivotal role in the assembly of PtdIns3K complexes, which is not the case for either FIP200 or ATG16L (Popli et al., 2022; Fan et al., 2011; Diao et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Popli et al., 2022; Fan et al., 2011; Diao et al., 2015.

claim: The retention of preimplantation embryos in the oviduct has been established as a significant contributor to implantation failures.
source: The retention of preimplantation embryos in the oviduct has been established as a significant contributor to implantation failures, presenting challenges to the overall reproductive health of women (Herrera et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2004; Qian et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Herrera et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2004; Qian et al., 2018.

claim: Embryo transport in the oviduct is known to be controlled primarily by two major physiological responses: ciliary activity and muscle contractility.
source: Embryo transport in the oviduct is known to be controlled primarily by two major physiological responses: ciliary activity and muscle contractility.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of oviduct physiology.

claim: Cilia are dispensable for embryo transport in the oviduct.
source: Although unexpected, this is consistent with other reports that have demonstrated the dispensability of cilia for embryo transport in the oviduct (Herrera et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Herrera et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2004.

claim: Pyroptosis is characterized by cell swelling, flattening of the cytoplasm, and large bubbles-like protrusions on the plasma membrane.
source: Pyroptosis is a highly inflammatory form of programmed cell death, characterized by cell swelling, flattening of the cytoplasm, and large bubbles-like protrusions on the plasma membrane (Ma et al., 2021; Cookson and Brennan, 2001; Jorgensen and Miao, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ma et al., 2021; Cookson and Brennan, 2001; Jorgensen and Miao, 2015.

claim: Autophagy is modulated in the human endometrium during the menstrual cycle.
source: Previous reports indicated that autophagy is modulated in the human endometrium during the menstrual cycle.
evidence: Based on previous literature on autophagy in endometrium.

claim: Autophagy is altered during the proliferative and secretory phases of the menstrual cycle with its highest activity occurring during the secretory phase when the stroma is decidualized.
source: For example, autophagy is altered during the proliferative and secretory phases of the menstrual cycle with its highest activity occurring during the secretory phase when the stroma is decidualized (Choi et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Choi et al., 2014.

claim: The level of autophagy was higher in postmenopausal human uterine epithelial cells compared to premenopausal uterine epithelial cells.
source: Similarly, the level of autophagy was higher in postmenopausal human uterine epithelial cells compared to premenopausal uterine epithelial cells, indicating the onset of autophagy upon estrogen deprivation (Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2020.

claim: ~20–25 embryos were recovered from super-ovulated cKO mice oviducts at day 4 of pregnancy.
source: Similarly, when we super-ovulated the mice and looked for the embryos on day 4 of pregnancy, we could recover ~20–25 embryos from the cKO mice oviducts compared to only 4–5 embryos that were able to reach the uterus.
evidence: Supported by embryo flushing data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Only 4–5 embryos were able to reach the uterus in super-ovulated cKO mice at day 4 of pregnancy.
source: Similarly, when we super-ovulated the mice and looked for the embryos on day 4 of pregnancy, we could recover ~20–25 embryos from the cKO mice oviducts compared to only 4–5 embryos that were able to reach the uterus.
evidence: Supported by embryo flushing data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In super-ovulated control mice, 90% of embryos were able to complete their predestined and timely transport to the uterus.
source: In comparison, in control mice, 90% of embryos were able to complete their predestined and timely transport to the uterus (Figure 3E), except 1–2% of unfertilized embryos, which remained in their oviducts.
evidence: Supported by embryo flushing data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: 1–2% of unfertilized embryos remained in the oviducts of super-ovulated control mice.
source: In comparison, in control mice, 90% of embryos were able to complete their predestined and timely transport to the uterus (Figure 3E), except 1–2% of unfertilized embryos, which remained in their oviducts.
evidence: Supported by embryo flushing data shown in Figure 3E.
